records.name: Equal-circle packing in a square
records.definition: Place n congruent disks without overlap in a square and minimize the square side (equivalently maximize the common disk radius in a unit square).
records.solution_format: disk centers and radius, or normalized center coordinates
records.scalar_objective: maximum common radius in unit square (equivalently minimum container side for unit disks)
records.configuration_parameters: n; fixed unit-square container; rotations irrelevant
records.human_baseline: Packomania lists best-known values, coordinates, drawings, contact graphs, and attribution codes for n up to 10000; it marks proven optima. Human attribution in records, AI involvement unknown.
records.verification_cost: medium; pairwise distance and wall-clearance checks; upper-bound optimality is generally hard
records.risks: Packomania is a changing best-known catalogue, not a proof for most n; choose frozen version/instances and verify contact tolerances.
records.reason: Named classical continuous optimization problem, dense public records and coordinates, natural scalar objective.

records.human_baseline: Packomania's catalogue is complete through N=2600, includes coordinates/contact graphs, and identifies proven optima and active historical researchers; AI involvement unknown.
records.verification_cost: medium; distance and containment checks; proving best-known optimality is harder
records.risks: Many entries are records rather than proven optima; source updates frequently.
records.reason: Strong named archive and solution artefacts; use fixed n and distinguish feasible record from certified optimum.

records.name: Packing unit squares in squares

records.risks: Do not treat upper-bound construction as proven optimum except rows marked/proven in the paper; use exact coordinate reconstruction.
records.reason: Named longstanding problem, unusually clear human history, explicit scalar and published benchmark range.

records.risks: Umbrella over different domains; no record values verified, not a single task.
records.reason: Use only after choosing and verifying one domain-specific benchmark with human records.

records.name: Unit-square coverings with varying tile inventory
records.definition: Given n unit squares, maximize the area of an axis-aligned square covered by their union, allowing overlaps and arbitrary rotations as in Friedman–Paterson.
records.solution_format: unit-square poses and target square
records.configuration_parameters: n; unit square tiles
records.human_baseline: Friedman–Paterson report known exact cases n=2,3,5,10 and n square, plus best-known bounds/constructions for others.
records.verification_cost: medium
records.risks: Duplicate of geo-unit-square-cover-square under alternate wording.
records.reason: Duplicate; keep the established entry once.

records.name: Largest circle covered by n squares
records.definition: Place n unit squares to cover a circular target of maximum radius.
records.solution_format: square placements and target circle
records.configuration_parameters: n; unit squares; overlaps allowed
records.human_baseline: Friedman catalog page for Squares Covering Circles exists, but it was not opened for named results in this audit; unknown.
records.verification_cost: medium
records.risks: Same as geo-squares-cover-circle; duplicate phrasing.
records.reason: Duplicate candidate and baseline not checked.

records.name: Distribute points in a square with maximum separation
records.definition: Choose n centers in a unit square to maximize the least clearance among all pairs and from the boundary, as the circle-center equivalent of equal-disk packing.
records.solution_format: n center coordinates
records.scalar_objective: minimum of pair separation and twice boundary clearance (equivalent radius scale)
records.configuration_parameters: n; unit square; boundary clearance included
records.human_baseline: Packomania explicitly describes equal-circle packing in a square as equivalent to distributing the centers in a square and provides a large best-known record table with downloadable coordinates.
records.verification_cost: low
records.risks: Equivalent scalar must be correctly normalized; do not use pairwise distance alone.
records.reason: Mathematically valid reparameterization but duplicate of equal-circle-in-square rather than a separate task.

records.name: Tammes problem / spherical codes
records.definition: Place N points on S² to maximize their minimum pairwise angular separation (equivalently chord distance).
records.solution_format: N unit vectors
records.configuration_parameters: N; dimension 3 for cited tables
records.human_baseline: Henry Cohn’s table lists constructions through N=32 with nearest-pair inner products and rattler counts; Sloane’s tables include downloadable coordinates. Records are not all proven optima. Historical human attribution; AI use unknown.
records.verification_cost: Low for feasibility; global optimality is hard.
records.risks: Use a frozen N row and report best-known versus proven status; do not count distinct container variants as separate tasks.
records.reason: Named problem, public coordinates, natural scalar.

records.name: Riesz energy minimization on the sphere (Thomson at s=1)
records.definition: For fixed N points on S², minimize the sum over unordered pairs of distance raised to −s; Thomson is s=1.
records.solution_format: N unit vectors / coordinate file
records.configuration_parameters: N and exponent s; fix s=1 for Thomson
records.human_baseline: Cambridge Riesz Energy Database, s=1, lists 53 lowest-known minima for N=512–9913, with energy, symmetry, and downloadable coordinates; N=512 energy 124673.9055677. These are lowest located minima, not all certified global minima. AI use unknown.
records.verification_cost: Low-medium; evaluate all pair terms with suitable precision.
records.risks: Freeze N,s and do not call a located minimum globally optimal without proof.
records.reason: Maintained data has exact coordinate files and natural energy scalar; genuinely different from Tammes.

records.name: Minimum-size spherical t-design
records.definition: For fixed dimension and strength t, find an equal-weight spherical t-design using the fewest points.
records.solution_format: point coordinates plus moment identities/certificate
records.configuration_parameters: fix dimension d and strength t; S² is the best documented library
records.human_baseline: Hardin–Sloane library provides putatively optimal designs and coordinates. Their paper reports a 24-point 7-design first found by McLaren (1963), and records existence/minimal-size claims; it explicitly distinguishes analytic proofs from numerical coordinates. AI use unknown.
records.verification_cost: Medium-high; check all polynomial moments, with exactness needed for a proof.
records.risks: Small residual is not proof of exact design or minimum N; choose rows with exact coordinates and lower-bound certificate.
records.reason: Natural integer objective and public constructions, but per-instance proof/verification burden is high.

records.name: Maximum-volume polytope with N vertices on a sphere
records.definition: Choose at most N vertices on the unit sphere in R³ to maximize convex-hull volume.
records.solution_format: unit-vector coordinates / named polyhedron
records.configuration_parameters: vertex cap N; unit sphere in R³
records.human_baseline: Sloane tables include maximal-volume arrangements and downloadable coordinates. A 2026 paper resolves N=9 exactly: volume 3√(2√3−3), attained by a triaugmented triangular prism of specified shape. Human theorem and construction; AI use unknown.
records.verification_cost: Medium to calculate hull volume; optimum proof depends on N.
records.risks: Clarify at-most versus exactly N vertices. N=9 is a calibration, not open discovery.
records.reason: Distinct natural volume objective with an exact value and explicit human construction.

records.name: Heilbronn problem for a free convex region
records.definition: Place N points in any unit-area convex region to maximize the smallest triangle area among triples, normalized by the convex hull area.
records.solution_format: point coordinates
records.scalar_objective: minimum triple triangle area divided by convex-hull area
records.configuration_parameters: N; convex hull is free and normalized to area 1
records.human_baseline: Tej Stead’s table provides coordinates and a rational-arithmetic verifier. For N=8, A=0.0800001393294664…; David Cantrell found the construction (2007), and Tej Stead proved optimality (2026). The value is the root of 2060x^5−2332x^4+1064x^3−240x^2+26x−1.
records.verification_cost: Low for candidate coordinates; upper-bound proof varies by N.
records.risks: Living page has later AI-assisted records; use N=8 and label provenance explicitly.
records.reason: Specific human construction, proof, coordinates, natural scalar.

records.name: Minimum maximum-to-minimum pair-distance ratio
records.definition: Choose N points in R^d to minimize maximum pair distance divided by minimum pair distance; scale and translation are immaterial.
records.solution_format: N coordinates
records.scalar_objective: max pair distance / min pair distance
records.configuration_parameters: N,d; choose 2D N=5 or 7 for proved records
records.human_baseline: Friedman’s records state r²=(3+√5)/2 for N=5 and r²=4 for N=7, proved by Bateman and Erdős (1951); N=8 is proved by Bezdek and Fodor (1999). Diagrams are published. Newer rows include 2026 contributors; AI use there unknown.
records.verification_cost: Low for a candidate; global optimum proof hard for larger N.
records.risks: Do not constrain points to an arbitrary box; avoid recent AI-assisted rows if using a human-only baseline.
records.reason: Named problem with direct ratio objective and human-proved values.

records.name: Kissing number arrangements
records.definition: In dimension d, maximize the number of unit balls tangent to a central unit ball without interior overlap.
records.solution_format: contact directions / unit vectors
records.configuration_parameters: dimension d; use exact cases 3,4,8,24
records.human_baseline: Henry Cohn maintains best lower/upper bounds and archived configurations. Exact human results: τ3=12 (Schütte–van der Waerden, 1953), τ4=24 (Musin, 2003/08), τ8=240 and τ24=196560 (Odlyzko–Sloane / Levenshtein); latter configurations are D4/E8/Leech lattice vectors.
records.verification_cost: Low for feasibility; upper-bound proof can be very high.
records.risks: A construction establishes a lower bound only. Use proved dimensions for calibration and separate candidate count from optimum claims.
records.reason: Natural integer scalar and explicit, human-proven arrangements.

records.name: Minimum-dilation triangulation
records.definition: For a fixed point set, triangulate it to minimize the maximum ratio of triangulation shortest-path distance to straight-line distance over all point pairs.
records.solution_format: triangulation edge list
records.configuration_parameters: Point set; 2014 library has 210 instances with 10–70 points
records.human_baseline: UNICAMP archive provides 210 MDTP instances and results for Brandt, Gaiowski, de Rezende, de Souza (2014). Fekete, Keldenich, Perk (SoCG 2025) give exact algorithms and optimal regular n-gon results through n=100, with methods up to 30,000 points.
records.verification_cost: Medium-high; all-pairs paths and accurate sums of radicals.
records.risks: Do not assume every instance has certified optimum; use published exact instances/results or compare feasible values with bounds.
records.reason: Named task has public instance/results packages, substantial human baseline, natural scalar.

records.name: Minimum-weight triangulation
records.definition: Triangulate a fixed planar point set with straight edges minimizing the sum of edge lengths.
records.solution_format: triangulation edge list
records.configuration_parameters: point set; no Steiner vertices; hull edges included
records.human_baseline: Haas (SoCG 2018) reports certified optima on public benchmark classes up to 30 million uniform/normal points, TSPLIB up to 85,900, and VLSI up to 744,710; earlier Beirouti–Snoeyink exact uniform cases reached 80,000. Human algorithmic records; AI use unknown.
records.verification_cost: Medium to compute edge sum; global optimum is NP-hard in general.
records.risks: Need match a source instance to its solution/certificate. Never use uncertified inner optimum as answer.
records.reason: Strong natural task and human results, but this pass did not verify a convenient instance/solution archive.

records.name: Minimum convex partition of a polygon
records.definition: Partition a simple polygon into as few convex pieces as possible using noncrossing cuts.
records.solution_format: noncrossing diagonals or convex piece vertex lists
records.configuration_parameters: Fix polygon and specify Steiner-point/cut conventions; default diagonal-only
records.human_baseline: Published exact and integer-programming formulations exist, but a standardized public instance corpus with per-instance human values was not verified in this audit. Baseline unknown.
records.verification_cost: Low for checking a proposed partition; proving minimum is harder.
records.risks: Different Steiner/cut conventions define different tasks; clarify before admitting. Do not conflate with a coverage-feasibility problem.
records.reason: Natural scalar exists but public baseline and exact formulation need further source audit.

records.name: Lowest-order simple perfect squared square
records.definition: Tile a square by distinct integer-sided smaller squares, with no proper squared-rectangle subpattern, minimizing the number of component squares.
records.solution_format: Bouwkamp code or exact tile placements
records.configuration_parameters: One square; all tile sizes distinct; simple dissection
records.human_baseline: Duijvestijn discovered the unique order-21, side-112 simple perfect squared square by computer in 1978; squaring.net publishes its 21-tile code and states order 21 is minimal and unique. Explicit computer-assisted historical human construction.
records.verification_cost: Low-medium; exact integer tiling and distinct sizes; global proof is enumeration-based.
records.risks: Use side 112 record as calibration; higher order can have smaller side (110), so objective is order, not side length.
records.reason: Named dissection, exact natural integer objective, public construction code, proof of minimality.

records.name: Mrs. Perkins’s quilt
records.definition: For fixed n×n square, dissect into the fewest smaller integer-sided squares whose side lengths have gcd 1.
records.solution_format: integer square tiling / side lengths and positions
records.configuration_parameters: Fix outer side n; integer alignment; tile-side gcd 1
records.human_baseline: For n=13, the catalogue gives an optimal 11-square dissection with sides 1,1,2,2,2,3,3,4,6,6,7; no fewer than 11 is possible. Squaring.net lists results through n=120, while warning most later rows are best known rather than proven. Conway, Guy, Gay, Pegg and computer searches are documented.
records.verification_cost: Low for a proposed tiling/gcd; exact minimality varies by n.
records.risks: Use proven n=13 calibration; do not claim later best-known values are optimal.
records.reason: Explicit human layout, natural integer objective, clear proof status.

records.name: Klarner order of a polyomino
records.definition: For a fixed polyomino P, find the fewest congruent copies (translations, rotations, reflections allowed) that tile any rectangle.
records.solution_format: rectangle dimensions and copy placements
records.scalar_objective: minimum number of copies of P
records.configuration_parameters: fixed polyomino shape; allowed orientations stated
records.human_baseline: polyominoes.org lists P-pentomino order 2 and an explicit 2×5 tiling. The Handbook of Discrete and Computational Geometry defines order and records a Y-pentomino’s 5×10 rectangle (10 copies), with results by Klarner and Reid.
records.verification_cost: Low for a placement; proving no smaller order may require exhaustive search.
records.risks: Shape P is an instance parameter; P-pentomino order 2 is trivial. Use only a nontrivial shape with source-supported minimality.
records.reason: Named scalar problem and constructions exist, but candidate shapes and optimality evidence require selection.

records.name: Moving sofa problem
records.definition: Find the largest-area planar shape that can move by rigid motions through a unit-width right-angle hallway.
records.solution_format: analytic boundary arcs and continuous motion path
records.configuration_parameters: hallway width 1; one 90-degree turn
records.human_baseline: Gerver’s 18-arc shape has area 2.21953166887197… (1992). Jineon Baek’s 2024 work proves Gerver’s shape attains the maximum and gives analytic construction/proof. Solved human calibration.
records.verification_cost: Very high; continuous path containment and transcendental boundary equations.
records.risks: Admit only if symbolic/certified artifacts can be checked; not a simple verifier task.
records.reason: Excellent solved construction benchmark, but geometry certificate cost is unusually high.

records.name: Ambidextrous moving sofa
records.definition: Maximize area of a shape that can navigate a unit-width right-angle hallway in both directions.
records.solution_format: boundary plus two continuous admissible motion paths
records.configuration_parameters: hallway width 1; bidirectional passage constraint
records.human_baseline: Romik’s candidate has area about 1.6449552184. Its optimality remains open; a 2026 working repository explicitly labels candidate evidence separately from proved statements. Human candidate; no AI-free claim verified.
records.verification_cost: Very high; both continuous paths and area need certification.
records.risks: Working/research repository is not a settled optimum; no rigorous standard coordinate artifact checked.
records.reason: Natural scalar and human candidate exist, but weak baseline maturity and high verification cost.

records.name: Orchard planting / maximum 3-rich lines
records.definition: For N planar points, maximize the number of distinct lines containing exactly three points, under the source’s general-position convention.
records.solution_format: point coordinates and counted lines
records.configuration_parameters: N fixed; exact-three incidence convention
records.human_baseline: Sloane’s A003035 table gives values (e.g. N=7→6, 11→16, 14→26); cubic-curve constructions by Burr, Grünbaum and Sloane provide explicit examples. 2026 work gives t3(15)=31 and excludes 32 with a certificate. Historical human constructions; newer computational component identified.
records.verification_cost: Medium; exact collinearity/incidence checks.
records.risks: Exactly-three lines differs from number of collinear triples; pin down treatment of four-point lines and cite the coordinate file for chosen N.
records.reason: Named integer optimization and public historical values, but a reusable coordinate record for exact selected N needs audit.

records.name: Largest point set with no empty convex hexagon
records.definition: Find a largest finite point set in general position with no empty convex 6-gon.
records.solution_format: point coordinates
records.configuration_parameters: forbidden polygon size 6; no three collinear
records.human_baseline: Overmars (2003) found 29 points with no empty hexagon. Gerken and Nicolás proved every 30-point set contains one, so optimum is 29. A public paper gives the construction/search; formal verification work supplies a SAT certificate for the upper bound. Human result with computer-assisted search/proof.
records.verification_cost: Low for candidate set; global upper proof is high.
records.risks: Solved calibration; retrieve point coordinates from Overmars paper/data before admitting.
records.reason: Exact maximum, named construction, natural cardinality scalar.

records.name: Largest isosceles-triangle-free subset of an integer grid
records.definition: For fixed n, choose the largest subset of [n]² with no three distinct points forming any isosceles triangle, including collinear equally spaced triples.
records.solution_format: integer coordinate list
records.configuration_parameters: grid side n; exact arithmetic; degenerate isosceles triples forbidden
records.human_baseline: The public record page says the prior n=100 record was 160 from PatternBoost before AlphaEvolve raised it to 164; AlphaEvolve also found 112 for n=64. Repository has data/verifier. Baseline is explicitly AI/LLM-assisted, not human-only.
records.verification_cost: Low; exact squared-distance tests over triples.
records.risks: Existing AI benchmark contamination and no clean human-only incumbent; do not misstate provenance.
records.reason: Natural scalar/public verifier, but AI-assisted baseline conflicts with strict human-baseline requirement.

records.name: Largest small n-gon
records.definition: Among convex n-gons of diameter at most 1, maximize area.
records.solution_format: cyclic vertex coordinates with diameter normalized
records.configuration_parameters: n vertices; diameter bound 1; convexity
records.human_baseline: Reinhardt (1922) proved regular n-gons optimal for every odd n. Exact/global records also exist for n=4,6,8,10,12; Henrion–Messine used GloptiPoly for n=10,12 with global/numerical guarantees, and Audet et al. gave exact algebraic equations for small even cases.
records.verification_cost: Low for area/diameter/convexity; global certificate specialized.
records.risks: Choose a fixed n and distinguish proof from local numerical record.
records.reason: Named extremal task, natural area scalar, many concrete human results.

records.name: Erdős minimum distinct-distance problem
records.definition: For a fixed N, choose N distinct planar points that determine as few distinct positive pairwise Euclidean distances as possible.
records.solution_format: N point coordinates; normalize by similarity
records.configuration_parameters: N; Euclidean plane; arbitrary point coordinates
records.human_baseline: Erdős (1946) introduced D(N). A square lattice construction gives O(N/sqrt(log N)) distinct distances for square-grid sizes; Guth and Katz (Annals 2015) prove every N-point planar set determines at least cN/log N distances. For N=4 a square gives exactly 2 distances and is a simple exact calibration. AI use unknown for historical constructions.
records.verification_cost: Low for a fixed exact/rational coordinate set; global optimum proof is hard.
records.risks: A construction yields an upper bound on the minimum, not a proof of optimality. Use exact small-N calibration or compare distinct-distance count only; do not require an uncertified inner optimum.
records.reason: Distinct natural integer objective and major human construction/theorem history, but public coordinate/result benchmark files were not verified here.

records.name: (d,g)-cage order
records.definition: For fixed degree d and girth g, find the smallest order n of a d-regular graph of girth exactly g.
records.solution_format: Adjacency list/matrix of a d-regular graph with a verifiable girth certificate; objective is vertex count.
records.human_baseline: Exoo, Jajcay, Goedgebeur et al. (2025 preprint) improved eleven upper bounds; e.g. n(4,10)≤320. Exoo–Jajcay (2013) survey distinguishes known cages from upper-bound constructions; optimality is proved only for some parameter pairs.
records.verification_cost: Medium for a supplied graph; high to prove global minimality.
records.risks: Report incumbent order separately from proven minimum; exact optimality certificates are often absent.
records.reason: Natural scalar objective, rich named record tables, and independently checkable graph witnesses.

records.name: Degree–diameter problem
records.definition: For maximum degree d and diameter k, maximize the order of a simple graph.
records.solution_format: Graph adjacency list plus proof/check of maximum degree and diameter; objective vertex count.
records.human_baseline: The large degree/diameter graph table (Miller, Širáň and contributors; updated tables) records best known orders and marks the few proven optimal cases; Moore bound is an upper bound, not an attained baseline.
records.verification_cost: Medium for witness; exact optimum usually unknown.
records.risks: Must label best-known vs proven; table updates and graph conventions (regular vs maximum degree) need freezing.
records.reason: A clear extremal objective and extensive human constructions; feasible to score witness size.

records.name: Classical Ramsey number lower-bound construction
records.definition: For fixed s,t, construct the largest N-vertex graph with neither an s-clique nor an independent t-set, equivalently improve the lower bound R(s,t)≥N+1.
records.solution_format: Graph adjacency list; independently verify forbidden-clique/independent-set conditions; scalar N.
records.human_baseline: Exoo et al. (1997) catalogued 656 nonisomorphic (5,5,42)-graphs, implying R(5,5)≥43; Radziszowski Dynamic Survey rev. 18 (2026) records 43≤R(5,5)≤46, with the upper bound by Angeltveit–McKay (2024).
records.verification_cost: High; exact clique and independence checks scale exponentially, though certificates are finite and reproducible.
records.risks: A one-unit increase is meaningful but only if exact validation is performed; do not score heuristic estimates or claim exact Ramsey values from a lower-bound witness.
records.reason: Excellent human baseline and natural scalar, but restrict to modest s,t and require exact verifier/certificate.

records.name: Graph Ramsey number R(G,H)
records.definition: Minimum N such that every red/blue coloring of K_N contains red G or blue H; candidates can instead give certified lower-bound colorings on N−1 vertices.
records.solution_format: Edge coloring of K_N−1; objective largest certified coloring order.
records.human_baseline: Radziszowski Dynamic Survey DS1 (rev. 18, 2026) and Exoo construction tables contain published values and lower-bound colorings.
records.verification_cost: High but finite for lower-bound witness; exact value requires separate upper-bound proof.
records.risks: Overlaps classical Ramsey task; keep only non-clique forbidden graphs if parameterized as a distinct task family. Exact score cannot be claimed from coloring alone.
records.reason: Strong literature, but merge with classical Ramsey unless benchmark specifically fixes arbitrary graph pairs.

records.name: Turán number ex(n,K_r)
records.definition: Maximize edges in an n-vertex K_r-free graph.
records.solution_format: Simple graph adjacency list; objective edge count.
records.human_baseline: Turán's theorem (1941) exactly gives the balanced complete (r−1)-partite graph and edge count for all n,r; a calibration item with a formula, not a frontier challenge.
records.verification_cost: Low for candidate graph; proving optimality is theorem-level but formula is known.
records.risks: Too formulaic for a discovery benchmark; use only calibration, not novelty leaderboard.
records.reason: Natural scalar and exact human baseline, but classic cases have closed-form solutions.

records.name: Zarankiewicz number Z_{s,t}(m,n)
records.definition: Maximize edges in a bipartite graph with part sizes m,n containing no K_{s,t}.
records.solution_format: Bipartite adjacency matrix; objective number of 1 entries.
records.human_baseline: Published exact values and bounds are surveyed in the extremal graph literature; small square cases have SAT-verified tables (Mubayi et al. / 2022 SAT study corrects known table errors). Explicit finite-field constructions give human lower bounds.
records.verification_cost: Medium for forbidden biclique and edge count; optimality high.
records.risks: Older tables contain errors; pin a source version and instance. General asymptotics remain open.
records.reason: Clean extremal scalar, abundant constructions, and small instances admit exact machine checks.

records.name: Hypergraph Turán number ex_r(n,F)
records.definition: Maximize edges in an r-uniform n-vertex hypergraph avoiding a fixed forbidden r-graph F.
records.solution_format: List of r-subsets; objective edge count.
records.human_baseline: Keevash's survey and the Erdős problems archive record open cases and constructions. The 3-uniform K4 problem has Turán's construction at density 5/9, but exact density remains open; finite n entries can have exact/conjectured distinctions.
records.verification_cost: High; checking F-freeness is manageable for small n, global optimality is difficult.
records.risks: Do not blur finite exact values with asymptotic Turán density; choose frozen small n and explicit F.
records.reason: Canonical research problem with natural edge-count objective and published constructions/bounds.

records.name: Graph saturation number sat(n,F)
records.definition: Minimize edges in an n-vertex F-saturated graph: it is F-free, but adding any missing edge creates F.
records.solution_format: Graph adjacency list; objective edge count.
records.human_baseline: Bollobás (1965) initiated the problem; for cliques, classical constructions and recent papers give exact formulas for many ranges. Current papers state the standard definition and bounds.
records.verification_cost: Medium for candidate; exact optimum often requires proof.
records.risks: Newer specific F parameter results must be checked against publication status; easy families have formulaic answers.
records.reason: Natural minimization objective with established theory; curate a small frozen set of nontrivial F,n cases.

records.name: Maximum order of a Ramsey (s,t)-graph
records.definition: For fixed s,t, maximize n such that a graph on n vertices has clique number <s and independence number <t.
records.solution_format: Graph adjacency matrix; objective order n.
records.human_baseline: McKay's ANU computational Ramsey database includes explicit graphs and describes the largest known Ramsey graphs; the optimum is R(s,t)−1.
records.verification_cost: High for maximality; graph witness checks can be expensive.
records.risks: Equivalent to classical Ramsey lower-bound construction; merge into that row to avoid duplicate benchmark.
records.reason: Duplicate formulation of the same Ramsey objective; retain one canonical task.

records.name: Small regular graph of given girth (cage variants)
records.definition: Construct a small d-regular graph of girth at least g, possibly with extra restrictions such as bipartite or vertex-transitive.
records.solution_format: Graph; minimize order.
records.human_baseline: Exoo–Jajcay dynamic cage survey and House of Graphs record tables catalog constructions, with restrictions treated separately in papers.
records.verification_cost: Medium.
records.risks: This is the cage family; do not count variants as separate tasks unless added restriction is canonical and independently studied.
records.reason: Parameter/restriction variants of the cage task should be merged.

records.name: Maximum edges under prescribed girth
records.definition: For fixed n and girth threshold g, maximize edges in an n-vertex graph with girth at least g.
records.solution_format: Graph adjacency list; objective edge count.
records.human_baseline: Erdős–Sachs (1963) established existence of regular graphs of prescribed degree and girth; the cage survey provides named extremal records, but exact max-edge records for this broader fixed-n formulation were not curated in this pass.
records.verification_cost: Medium for girth and edge count; optimum difficult.
records.risks: A general problem family with sparse centralized records; source and exact instance baseline still need checking.
records.reason: Broad formulation lacks a verified standard human record table; cage records cover the stronger canonical family.

records.name: Maximum independence number under graph constraints
records.definition: Given a fixed graph class or forbidden subgraph family and order n, maximize alpha(G).
records.solution_format: Graph witness; objective independence number.
records.human_baseline: Many individual extremal results exist, but no unified, verified baseline database for arbitrary constraints was established in this survey pass.
records.verification_cost: High: exact maximum independent set is NP-hard; validating claimed alpha needs a matching upper certificate.
records.risks: Too broad; do not score a heuristic alpha estimate as exact.
records.reason: No single canonical family or practical human baseline; verification burden is high.

records.name: Saturated graph construction for fixed F
records.definition: Find an F-saturated graph with few edges on n vertices.
records.solution_format: Graph witness; objective edge count.
records.human_baseline: See sat(n,F) literature, but duplicates the saturation number task.
records.verification_cost: Medium.
records.risks: Duplicate formulation.
records.reason: Merge into canonical saturation-number task.

records.name: Covering number C(v,k,t)
records.definition: Find the fewest k-subsets of a v-set such that every t-subset is included in at least one selected block.
records.solution_format: List of k-subsets; objective block count.
records.human_baseline: La Jolla Combinatorics Repository (Dan Gordon; frozen 2026) stores tens of thousands of best-known covers and lower bounds; individual construction records identify contributors/methods.
records.verification_cost: Low-medium for coverage; proving minimum needs lower bound.
records.risks: Repository baseline may be best-known rather than optimum; freeze data snapshot and preserve authorship metadata.
records.reason: One of the strongest candidates: standardized finite objects, natural scalar, and large human record corpus.

records.name: Covering array CAN(t,k,v)
records.definition: Minimize rows N of a k-column v-ary array so every t selected columns contain every v^t tuple at least once.
records.solution_format: N×k array over v symbols; objective N.
records.human_baseline: NIST Covering Array Library lists actual arrays for strengths 2–6 and 2–6 levels, plus best-known sizes to 20,000 columns (strength 2) and 10,000 (strengths 3–6); NIST and Colbourn records are human constructions/bounds.
records.verification_cost: Low for explicit array; minimum proof varies.
records.risks: Keep uniform alphabet case separate from variable-strength/general mixed-level variants; NIST best-known size tables do not always include arrays.
records.reason: Excellent benchmark corpus and easily verifiable scalar optimization.

records.name: Orthogonal array minimum-run construction
records.definition: For fixed strength t, levels and columns, construct an orthogonal array with the fewest rows (or maximize columns for fixed rows), each t-column tuple appearing equally often.
records.solution_format: Array with explicit index lambda; objective rows or columns, with one direction fixed per instance.
records.human_baseline: Neil Sloane's library contains 200+ explicit arrays; Eendebak–Schoen catalogue complete non-isomorphic arrays for selected small parameters. OA( N,k,s,t) must meet divisibility/Rao bounds.
records.verification_cost: Low for explicit array; minimality moderate/high.
records.risks: Do not conflate OA existence, maximum columns, and minimum-run objectives; fix one scalar per instance. Strength-2 binary OAs are essentially Hadamard matrices.

records.name: Steiner system block construction S(t,k,v)

records.name: Maximum number of mutually orthogonal Latin squares
records.definition: For order n, maximize the number of pairwise orthogonal Latin squares (MOLS).
records.solution_format: List of Latin squares; objective count.

records.name: Maximum Hadamard matrix order under a bound
records.definition: For a fixed search bound M, find the largest order h≤M for which a ±1 matrix has mutually orthogonal rows.
records.solution_format: Hadamard matrix; scalar order h.

records.name: Projective plane order search
records.definition: For a fixed cap q≤Q, find the largest order q for which a projective plane exists.
records.solution_format: Incidence matrix; scalar order q.

records.reason: Mostly existence and known algebraic construction; poor natural scalar task.

records.name: Optimal Golomb ruler length
records.definition: For m integer marks, place distinct marks so all positive pairwise differences are distinct and minimize the largest mark.
records.solution_format: Increasing integer mark list starting at 0; objective final mark.
records.human_baseline: Shearer (1990) exhaustively proved optimal lengths 127,151,177 for m=14,15,16; distributed.net completed proof of optimality through m=28 (2022 records), and CSPLib has the standard benchmark. Distinguish proven optima from larger-m best known rulers.
records.verification_cost: Low for ruler; optimality proof high for large m.
records.risks: Open sizes beyond proven range must be scored as incumbent length, not as proven optimum; preserve provenance and certificate status.
records.reason: Ideal scalar objective, a standard benchmark and exceptionally clear historical human record.

records.name: Difference triangle sets
records.definition: Construct several rows of marks with all within-row positive differences distinct globally; minimize maximum span under fixed row/mark counts.
records.solution_format: Rows of integer marks; objective maximum row span.
records.human_baseline: Published difference-triangle-set constructions and tabu search literature report best-known spans; Golomb rulers are the one-row special case.
records.verification_cost: Low for a witness.
records.risks: Overlaps Golomb ruler at r=1; careful definition variants (all differences vs row-tagged) must be frozen.
records.reason: A legitimate adjacent optimization family with published records, but merge one-row case into Golomb rulers.

records.name: Largest Sidon set in [n]
records.definition: Find the largest subset of {1,…,n} whose pairwise sums of distinct elements are all different (equivalently distinct positive differences).
records.solution_format: Sorted integer set; objective cardinality.
records.human_baseline: Erdős–Turán (1941) prove the maximum Sidon-set size in [n] is asymptotic to √n; Bose–Chowla (1962) give finite-field constructions. Specific finite-n exact maxima are not asserted here; use a verified construction/bound table before scoring exactness.
records.verification_cost: Low for witness; proof of maximum can be difficult.
records.risks: Terminology differs on allowing repeated summands; specify pairwise sums of distinct elements and distinct differences explicitly. Exact small-n baseline table still needs verification.
records.reason: Very natural scalar and classical constructions; source-level exact benchmark table needs checking.

records.name: Maximum cap set in F_3^n
records.definition: Find a largest subset of the vector space F_3^n containing no affine line (three distinct points summing to zero).
records.solution_format: Point list in F_3^n; objective cardinality.
records.human_baseline: Pellegrino (1970) proved maximum 20 for n=4. Kleinberg–Sawin–Speyer (2016) gave constructions and Ellenberg–Gijswijt (2017) exponential upper bound; human lower-bound records are published for higher n, with exact values limited.
records.verification_cost: Low for witness and no-line property; proving optimality difficult.
records.risks: Modern record tables may have changed; distinguish exact small dimensions from best-known lower bounds.
records.reason: Canonical additive extremal problem, clear point-count objective, and unusually visible human construction frontier.

records.name: Largest 3-term-progression-free subset of [n]
records.definition: Find a largest subset of {1,…,n} containing no nontrivial 3-term arithmetic progression.
records.solution_format: Integer set; objective cardinality.
records.human_baseline: Behrend (1946) gave classical constructions; exact small-n values are known computationally and Roth's theorem gives qualitative upper bounds. Pin exact-value source/version for each n.
records.verification_cost: Low for witness, exponential for maximality.
records.risks: Closely related to cap sets but distinct ambient group; avoid treating parameter variants as different tasks.
records.reason: Natural cardinality objective, but benchmark exact records need authoritative tables and manageable n.

records.name: Minimum difference basis for [n]
records.definition: Find a smallest set A of integers such that every integer 1,…,n is a difference of two elements of A.
records.solution_format: Sorted integer set; objective cardinality (or span if a different canonical version is chosen).
records.human_baseline: Difference-basis literature has asymptotic bounds and specific constructions (Rédei–Rényi; Leech), but this pass did not verify an accessible modern exact-record table.
records.verification_cost: Low for coverage; proving minimality difficult.
records.risks: Several inequivalent definitions (difference set vs difference basis, interval endpoint, signed differences); human baseline source requires additional research.
records.reason: Natural minimum-cardinality task but needs definition and authoritative record table curation.

records.name: Minimum additive basis of order h for [n]
records.definition: Find a smallest A⊂[0,m] or minimum largest element such that every target integer up to n is a sum of h elements of A (convention fixed).
records.solution_format: Integer set; objective cardinality or maximum element (choose one).
records.human_baseline: Classical additive-basis literature studies several nonequivalent variants; a specific finite database and baseline were not verified in this pass.
records.verification_cost: Low-medium for witness; proof of optimality hard.

records.name: Maximum sum-free subset of a finite group

records.definition: Maximize edges in an r-uniform n-vertex hypergraph with matching number below fixed s.

records.name: Schur number S(k) lower-bound coloring
records.definition: For fixed k colors, construct a coloring of [N] with no monochromatic x+y=z; maximize N, the certified lower bound for S(k).

records.verification_cost: Low for lower-bound coloring; proving exact value needs a large SAT/DRAT proof.

records.name: van der Waerden number lower-bound coloring
records.definition: For fixed r colors and AP length k, construct the longest r-coloring of [N] with no monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression.
records.solution_format: Coloring of [N]; scalar N.

records.reason: Natural construction objective with published numerical records and cheap witness validation.

records.name: Longest finite sequence with discrepancy at most C
records.definition: For a fixed discrepancy cap C, find the largest prefix length N of a ±1 sequence such that every homogeneous initial segment along every arithmetic progression has absolute sum at most C.
records.solution_format: Sign sequence of length N; exact scalar N.
records.human_baseline: Konev–Lisitsa (2015) reported a discrepancy-3 sequence of length 127,645, improving 17,000, with inductive construction rules; Tao (2015) proved the infinite Erdős discrepancy conjecture.
records.verification_cost: Low for a supplied finite sequence; proving maximality requires exhaustive/combinatorial upper certificates.
records.risks: The unbounded infinite theorem itself is not a finite optimization task; freeze exact prefix discrepancy convention and evaluate witness length only.
records.reason: A named finite extremal version has a concrete human record and exact scalar witness.

records.name: Ruzsa–Szemerédi (6,3) graph extremal number
records.definition: For fixed n, maximize the number of triples in a 3-uniform hypergraph on n vertices such that no six vertices contain three hyperedges (the Brown–Erdős–Sós (6,3) formulation).
records.solution_format: 3-uniform hyperedge list; objective number of hyperedges.
records.human_baseline: Ruzsa–Szemerédi (1976/1978) proved the maximum size of a 3-uniform (6,3)-free system is o(n²); Behrend-type constructions give n² exp(−O(√log n)) lower bounds. These are asymptotic human bounds; no exact finite record table asserted.
records.verification_cost: Medium for triangle incidence checks; extremality proof is difficult.
records.risks: Use the explicit hypergraph (6,3) definition: every three distinct edges span at least seven vertices. This avoids ambiguity with graph encodings where every edge belongs to a unique triangle.
records.reason: Canonical active extremal problem with natural scalar, pending verified instance-level numerical records.

records.name: Finite-set sum–product growth minimization
records.definition: For a fixed size m and a fixed ambient integer interval [B], find A⊂[B], |A|=m minimizing max(|A+A|,|A·A|), with operations in the integers.
records.solution_format: Finite integer set A; objective the larger of sumset/product-set cardinalities.
records.human_baseline: Erdős–Szemerédi (1983) established a power-growth theorem for integer sets; later Solymosi and others improve exponents. No canonical exact finite-n construction table for this min-max objective was verified in this pass.
records.verification_cost: Low for a finite set and exact integer operations; global optimum hard.
records.risks: Integer interval bound B affects the problem substantially and may be artificial; no verified human optimum table. Restrict to conditional exploratory instances only.
records.reason: A real finite optimization scalar, but a standardized published finite benchmark frontier was not confirmed.

records.name: Minimum diameter of a B_h set of integers, h≥3
records.definition: For fixed m and h≥3, choose m integers with all h-term sums (repetition convention fixed) distinct, minimizing the diameter.
records.solution_format: Sorted integer set; objective maximum minus minimum.
records.human_baseline: Bose–Chowla (1962) give finite-field B_h constructions; modern additive-combinatorics papers provide bounds. The h=2 case is the Golomb/Sidon ruler task and is deliberately excluded here as a duplicate.
records.verification_cost: Low for witness; exact optimum difficult.
records.risks: Must distinguish unordered multisets with repetitions from distinct-element sums and from modular B_h sets; h=2 merges with Golomb rulers.
records.reason: Natural generalization with human algebraic constructions; finite exact baselines need dedicated verification.

records.name: Minimum finite-field Kakeya set size
records.definition: For fixed finite field F_q and dimension d, minimize |K| over K⊂F_q^d containing a full affine line in every direction.
records.solution_format: Point list or characteristic function; objective |K|.
records.human_baseline: Dvir (2009) proved |K|≥c_d q^d by the polynomial method; explicit constructions are known. An October 2026 exposition reports an exact exhaustive result |K|=13 for F_3^3, but that source is secondary, so require primary-paper confirmation before adopting this numeric record.
records.verification_cost: Low for candidate set; exact minimum needs exhaustive or mathematical lower bound.
records.risks: Small finite cases and field characteristic matter; separate proven minimum from construction upper bound; record 2026 claim as pending primary confirmation.
records.reason: Natural finite extremal objective with strong theory, but exact record data are currently thin.

records.name: Arithmetic Kakeya covering-set size
records.definition: For a precisely fixed k-AP covering formulation, minimize the initial-segment count |A∩[N]| subject to A containing a translate of every required k-term arithmetic progression pattern/direction.

records.definition: Maximize |A| for A⊂[N] with no distinct a,b∈A such that |a−b| is a perfect square.

records.verification_cost: Low for a finite set; proof of maximum difficult.

records.verification_cost: Low for collinearity checks; optimum proof hard.

records.definition: Maximize points in an n×n integer grid subject to no three selected points forming an isosceles triangle (definition includes/excludes collinear triples explicitly).

records.name: Erdős–Szekeres happy-ending number f(k)
records.definition: Find the minimum N such that every N points in general position in the plane contain k points in convex position.

records.verification_cost: Geometric general-position and convexity checks are low with exact coordinates; upper proof is difficult.

records.name: Erdős Minimum Overlap
records.definition: Let f:[0,2]→[0,1] be a step function with ∫_0^2 f(x)dx=1. Define g(x)=1−f(x) for x∈[0,2] and g(x)=0 outside [0,2]. Minimize Ψ(f)=sup_{t∈R} ∫_R f(x)g(x+t)dx = sup_{t∈R} ∫_[0,2]∩[-t,2-t] f(x)(1−f(x+t))dx. Both f and g are zero outside [0,2]; this is essential. Include both shift directions and do not use finite M(N) as the same score.
records.solution_format: Exact rational step function with breakpoints and values, exact mass, and a rigorous maximization over all shifts s (piecewise polynomial plus root isolation/interval arithmetic).
records.scalar_objective: Ψ(f)=sup_{t∈R}∫_R f(x)g(x+t)dx, where f,g are supported on [0,2] and g=1−f on [0,2] (lower is better). Equivalent to the intersection-range integral; both positive and negative shifts are included.

configuration_parameters.step_count: number of equal-width intervals on [0,2] (e.g. 15 or 51); representation setting, not a separate task

records.human_baseline: Haugland (2016) reports human step-function upper-bound witnesses for this continuous normalized objective: 15 steps gives 0.38153155 (rounded upward); 51 steps gives 0.3809268534330870. These are reported construction scores, not independently reproduced here. AI-assisted results are separate.
records.verification_cost: Finite exact task low/medium; limiting witness high (integral/profile derivation and rigorous discretization error certificate).
records.risks: Both f and its complement g must be supported on [0,2], with g=1−f only inside [0,2] and zero outside. If 1−f is incorrectly zero-extended as a function equal to 1 outside, endpoint shifts spuriously score 1. Use sup over all real t, equivalently include both positive and negative shifts; a nonsymmetric candidate cannot be scored using only one shift direction. Certify the piecewise functional over every shift interval, not on a grid. The finite partition M(N)/N is related but not the same candidate score.
records.reason: Named limiting extremal problem with Haugland continuous step-function upper-bound constructions and a natural scalar. The support convention for both f and g makes the score well-defined and comparable to the published 0.38 values.

records.definition: For a fixed integer N, partition prime factors of N! among N integer factors and maximize the smallest factor; C(N) is the largest c for which N! can be factored into N factors all at least c.
records.solution_format: N positive integers with product exactly N!; verify exact product and minimum factor.
